evidence.im_comment: Evidence suggests advocating to weaken the EU Methane Regulation for the energy sector: emphasizing security of supply concerns with the regulation's 2027 requirements for importers (TotalEnergies, CEO, Patrick Pouyanné, Upstream, October 2025)
evidence.source_extract: The European Union should scrap methane and due diligence regulations to protect the bloc's supply of liquefied natural gas, Patrick Pouyanne, chief executive of TotalEnergies, said on Tuesday. From 2027, importers will have to ensure that LNG shipped into the EU complies with methane monitoring and reporting rules equivalent to EU regulations. Meanwhile the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) from 2027 will require importers to ensure that LNG imports meet EU climate and human rights laws. Pouyanne told delegates at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Tuesday that he had signed a letter, alongside 45 other industry chief executives, calling on the EU to scrap the methane regulations and CSDDD."The EU doesn't believe Qatar's Minister of Energy when he says he will not take the risk to sell LNG to Europe. They are wrong, he is very serious," Pouyanne told delegates at the conference on Tuesday. "But with the regulations we have a problem as we will go from one reliance on Russia to another reliance on the US." [...] EU plans to tackle methane emissions and guarantee human rights across the supply chain have been criticised by industry for hampering imports of LNG needed to bolster European energy security, and French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have both called for the CSDDD to be canned. "I know that President Macron would like to abolish the regulations but when he takes the train to Brussels, I think he seems to change his mind," Pouyanne said. "But security of supply is important in the narrative of Europe and I think they will become pragmatic on this one, because it's a huge issue," he said. European LNG importers could face fines of up to 20% of their annual turnover if they do not comply with new methane emissions rules or supply chain due diligence requirements under EU rules introduced over the past year but Pouyanne argued that the rules were unworkable, particularly in the US where it was difficult to provide accurate methane calculations at a field level.

evidence.source_extract: Speaking at a meeting of the EU Competitiveness Council in Brussels today (18 February), representatives from members of the Prince of Wales's Corporate Leaders Group (CLG) will argue that ambitious carbon reduction targets are the best way to secure the EU’s economic competitiveness. CLG's director Eliot Whittington is expected to tell policymakers representing EU member states at the meeting that a net-zero goal for 2050 would encourage investment in sustainable business while helping finance firms to avoid stranded assets and missed investment opportunities. He is also set to argue that the transition to a net-zero carbon economy will create opportunities which must be seized through collaboration between corporates and governments. These arguments, plus a string of recommendations as to how the net-zero policy framework should be set, will be presented to EU policymakers at the meeting. Specifically, the CLG is calling for the EU to consult businesses, investors, NGOs, local authorities and the general public on any targets it sets. This move, it argues, will ensure a “comprehensive and credible approach, which covers the whole of the economy and society”. The recommendations have received backing from all 16 of the CLG’s member corporates – Acciona, Anglian Water, Coca Cola European Partners, DSM, EDF, GlaxoSmithKline, Heathrow Airport, Iberdrola, Interface, Signify, Sky, StoraEnso, Tesco, Thames Water, Unilever and United Technologies. They additionally include a request for policymakers to conduct regular reviews of their national and EU-wide carbon targets, to ensure they align with wider economic, scientific and technological developments.

evidence.im_comment: Evidence suggests supporting the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and increasing the ETS's Linear Reduction Factor (Climate Policy Engagement Review, March 2024)
evidence.source_extract: Negative position on EU Emissions trading system (ETS) reform and the phase-in of a carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) CEFIC has pushed for an extension of free allowances under the EU ETS and a slower phase-in of CBAM. It has opposed proposals to a) increase the ETS’s Linear Reduction Factor (the rate at which the cap on GHG emissions decreases annually) and b) reduce the cap on total GHG emissions to zero by 2039. […] CEFIC’s lobbying on the EU ETS and CBAM is judged to be misaligned with Unilever’s goal of ensuring a meaningful price on carbon that reflects the full costs of climate change. This is because adoption of its proposals would lead to the carbon price paid by industries covered by the EU ETS remaining lower for longer compared with a scenario in which its proposals were not implemented. […] Its calls for ETS expansion and a tightening of emissions caps to drive up carbon prices is also consistent with Unilever’s position on the need for a meaningful price on carbon. […] The one area where ERT’s lobbying during 2022-23 appears to be misaligned is on carbon pricing. Its proposals for CO2 cost compensation and its implied opposition to tapering the free allocation of ETS allowances would mean the actual cost of emitting carbon (for companies covered by the EU ETS) would remain lower for longer than if its proposals were not adopted. ERT’s concerns about the impact on competitiveness and the problem of carbon leakage may be justified, but its proposals fail to address these concerns in a way that is consistent with the goal of pricing GHG emissions at a level that reflects the full costs of climate change.

[...] In addition to facilitating the use of the existing Clean Industry State Aid Framework (CISAF) mechanism for targeted electricity price relief for industry – while avoiding distortions to the electricity market – we encourage you to enable the efficient redistribution of EU ETS revenues to support industrial decarbonisation and electrification; - ensure efficient carbon leakage protection without undermining CBAM and the efficiency of the EU ETS; - swiftly establish the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank announced under the Clean Industrial Deal to support industries as they electrify.

evidence.im_comment: Advocating for the need for stringent policy interventions to support a rapid transition to renewables in the energy mix (Iberdrola, feedback on the EU's "Renewable energy – legal framework after 2030" consultation, April 2026)
evidence.source_extract: This revision takes place in a very specific context vis-à-vis previous revision cycles. While the EU is strengthening and aligning its long-term industrial and climate ambitions, the effects of the war in the Middle-East come once again to highlight the EU’s structural vulnerabilities linked to fossil fuel dependency. Against this backdrop, accelerating the deployment of renewable energy (and maintaining existing nuclear) is not only central to delivering on the EU’s decarbonisation trajectory but also key for safeguarding the EU’s competitiveness, resilience and strategic autonomy [...] At the heart of this transformation is electrification. Electrification of end uses powered by renewables is emerging as the most efficient, scalable and cost-effective pathway to enhance competitiveness, lower exposure to volatile energy markets and strengthen energy security. Mature and widely available solutions (such as heat pumps, low temperature heat for industries or electric mobility) demonstrate electrification is no longer a long-term aspiration but a near-term lever for EU’s objectives. To ensure the EU can meet its 2040 climate target and establish the foundations for a competitive, resilient and energy-independent economy, the revised RED must create a stable, coherent, predictable and derisk investment-friendly framework. This framework must accelerate renewable energy deployment across all sectors. This includes removing structural barriers, aligning the Directive with broader EU industrial and energy strategies, and prioritising electrification as the backbone of Europe’s clean-energy transition. The next phase of EU energy policy must therefore treat renewables not only as a climate imperative, but as a strategic asset for Europe’s prosperity and security in an increasingly unstable world. [...] 1) Maintain the current basic architecture: an EU-wide renewables target and national commitments to support the phase out of fossil fuels imports [...] 2) Integration of renewables: enablers for electrification of end uses, grids and non-fossil flexibility The RED should include the necessary enablers for the electrification of end uses, grid development and non-fossil flexibility. Particularly, this should include: • Network planning. It must be mandatory to align the network planning with electrification targets, non-fossil flexibility needs, and renewable objectives. • Electrification Acceleration Areas. This idea (i) builds on the Industrial Accelerator Areas proposed in the Industrial Accelerator Act, and (ii) would be part of the previously proposed national plans for the orderly phasing out of fossil fuels. In particular, these areas would allow to further coordinate the electrification of end uses and grid development with (i) the expansion of renewables and non-fossil flexibilities under the current Renewables Acceleration Areas approach and (ii) the phase out of fossil infrastructures. • Transport sector. The RED should explicitly include private charging in the accounting of renewable electricity in transport, thus avoiding distorting its contribution as it represents the majority of charging.

evidence.source_extract: Coal closures remain a critical unaddressed challenge […] Our primary concern is the lack of clear market signals for the closure of coal and the ongoing reliance on underwriting new entrant capacity rather than creating enduring, demand-side market signals for investment. Governments will naturally (and rightly) continue to want to see investment in new capacity ahead of coal closures. However, recent evidence suggests investors can have little certainty of announced coal closure dates (which may be earlier or later than anticipated). As such, until the majority of coal stations have closed, it is credible that near-term prices (e.g., years 1-7) will not be sufficient to justify investment. […] Capacity procurement should be linked to the requirements for the closure of the next coal unit. New capacity should be held into reserve until sufficient reserved capacity is available to close the next coal unit. At this point, the coal unit would be closed through regulation, and the reserve capacity brought into the market. This reserved capacity would act as capacity under the proposed Reserve Market, but with the added flexibility of smoothing the transition as coal plant exit. This would have the benefit of providing clear and transparent certainty to jurisdictions on coal closures and reducing an oversupplied market such that ESEM contracts could be priced more efficiently, while delivering identical reliability outcomes. […] Alternatively, we previously proposed a “Waiting Room” underwriting option for new entrant generation. Under this proposal, a transitional feature of the market would be for the procurement of replacement capacity in anticipation of coal closures. This could comprise energy storage (e.g., batteries), fuel-based firming capacity, and/or energy production (e.g., wind or solar).

evidence.im_comment: Supporting the EU's 2035 regulatory phase-out of ICE powered light-duty vehicles and the expansion of charging infrastructure through the EU's AFIR (Iberdrola, Comments on Revision of the CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, October 2025)
evidence.source_extract: We believe this legislative effort presents a unique opportunity to accelerate the decarbonisation of road transport while enhancing its competitiveness, resilience, and technological leadership. We suggest the following considerations for the Commission’s assessment: 1. Preserve ambition and regulatory certainty The current CO₂ standards have proven effective in reducing emissions and boosting the supply of zero-emission vehicles. We strongly support maintaining the 100% CO₂ reduction target for 2035 and the review timeline of end-2026. Avoiding exemptions for climateneutral fuels is essential; if introduced, they must be strictly limited to vehicles running exclusively on e-fuels, with robust safeguards. 2. Strengthen coherence with infrastructure deployment The ambition of CO₂ standards must be matched by the timely rollout of charging infrastructure. Stronger alignment with the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) is needed to ensure that vehicle targets are achievable in practice. 3. Improve and harmonise vehicle labelling The Car Labelling Directive must be updated to reflect market and technological developments. We recommend full harmonisation across Member States and the inclusion of relevant information for zero-emission vehicles (e.g. energy consumption, range, charging time, battery durability). 4. Support affordability and uptake of zero-emission vehicles We recommend a comprehensive set of complementary measures, including: • Direct purchase incentives, ideally tax-exempt. • Favourable taxation for electricity vs. fossil fuels. • Social leasing schemes for low-income users. • Electrification of corporate fleets to boost the second-hand EV market. • Urgent transposition of RED III to enable e-credits. • Simplification and acceleration of the processing for the installation and commissioning of all components of charging points.

evidence.im_comment: Supporting digitalisation, demand-side flexibility, and smart grids as core enablers of renewables integration and electrification; supporting measures to improve grid infrastructure, with reference to the need for increased clean energy transmission capacity (Iberdrola, Consultation response on the EU Grid Package, August 2025)
evidence.source_extract: Although wholesale market integration has advanced positively across the EU, with tangible results, there is large room for progress on the alignment of key elements of network regulation (e.g. planning, asset remuneration, investment limits, etc). Such misalignment affects EU economies in the transition towards electrification and climate neutrality challenges. The construction of interconnections should not hinge primarily on the political will of transit MSs, between net exporter countries and net importers. It is not a bilateral issue, but a central matter for the whole Single Market to succeed. [...] Transmission planning in Spain needs to be improved to balance generation and demand. This includes strengthening demand resources and better integrating DSO planning. Indeed, grids need to expand significantly to modernise and accommodate demand growth and new resources (distributed renewables, electric vehicle charging infrastructure) in a smart and digitalised way. In this context, MSs need to fully implement Directive (EU) 2019/944 regarding Distribution Network Development Plans within a 5-10-years horizon and adapt regulatory frameworks to enable anticipatory investments. Improper planning can lead to missed opportunities in terms of industrial grid connections which are, de facto, missed opportunities in terms of reindustrialisation of the EU. [...] The Distribution Network Development Plans - DNDPs [...] In this respect, anticipating future investments is an essential exercise to adequately address the needs of the different sectors (renewables, electromobility, heating and cooling, data centres among other sectors). It is important that all countries in the EU can implement DNDPs as defined in the Electricity Directive, enabling an assessment of medium to long-term network investments, ensuring the participation of stakeholders and the cooperation among system operators, which conveys the suppression of caps/limitation on investment in grids, as established in Spain (based on a percentage of GDP). [...] Shortening connection times depend on getting a simplified and digital permitting system and avoiding the shortage of connection capacity addressed. Necessary steps to accelerate connections and avoid speculative and immature applications stand on longterm anticipatory planning with no implicit or explicit cap. In addition, transmission planning and capacity allocation must be adapted to facilitate closer coordination between TSO-DSO ensuring that grid capacity is used and adapted more efficiently (rebalancing TSO priorities to shift towards supporting the demand growth). Connection queues could be mitigated through the implementation of flexible connection agreements, applicable to new capacity requests, as a temporary solution until the network reinforcements come online. The "first-come-first served" principle has played an important role to organize the connection requests, although there is room for improvement through the principle 'first-ready-first-served' approach: - Strengthen the credibility of requests - Generalize the requirement of economic guarantees to all requests for access and demand connection that connect to voltages larger than 1 kV - Faster expiration of connection permits (currently in Spain, up to 5 years). - Introduction of milestones and phases in the process of accessing and connecting to the network that would lead to the expiration of the application if they were not certified. - Introduction of prioritization criteria, such as: o Maturity of urban and industrial projects o Location in areas of preferential industrial or technological development (which makes them creditors of public funding). o Transport/service infrastructures with criteria of overriding public interest. All these criteria must be decided, analyzed and tracked by the regulatory authority. We strongly request that DSOs are not given the responsibility of deciding over these potentially contentious issues. [...] The development of distribution grids should be always classified as of overriding public interest. Most renewable development (fundamentally solar) is connected at distribution networks, which implies that the public interest in building distribution grids is no less than that of the construction of renewables. [...] Public funding's role could be oriented to the following paths: - support to cover the costs of electrification for residential customers, services, and industries. This contributes to increasing electricity demand and reduces increasing network costs among larger consumption. [...] [Q25: In your view, should there be further measures to increase the efficiency of the existing grid?] No

evidence.im_comment: Strongly supporting the EU initiative to scale up the CO2 transportation infrastructure and markets; supporting CCU/S and carbon removal (CDR) to compensate for residual emissions hard-to-abate sectors only (Iberdrola, Comments on the EU Legislative initiative on CO2 transportation infrastructure and markets, September 2025)
evidence.source_extract: Iberdrola supports the Industrial Carbon Management strategy, which establishes that (i) “CCS must be deployed at large scale to complement other mitigation actions to address hard to abate emissions, in particular industrial process emissions, and to achieve climate neutrality by 2050”, and (ii) “To reach net-zero economy-wide GHG emissions by 2050, the EU could need carbon removals to balance out around 400 million tonnes CO2 equivalent of residual emissions in hard-to-abate sectors such as agriculture, aviation and some industries”. Therefore: • CCSU and carbon removals are to target residual emissions once available efficient mitigation measures have been exhausted. [...] • Inefficient technologies should not be broadly promoted until their long-term role is clear and they reach sufficient technological maturity. [...] • The efficiency of the mitigation measures must be assessed internalizing the positive externality they create in terms of reducing the EU’s economy’s dependence on fossil fuels imports. [...] Under these criteria, and with a view of ensuring the development of competitive markets and efficient transportation infrastructure for CO2 under the energy system integration framework, Iberdrola suggests to develop impact assessments (IA) to ensure technical and economic feasibility, proportionality, and alignment with the objectives of the proposal. The IA should explore the most cost-effective route to (i) achieving net-zero emissions and (ii) reducing the EU’s economy’s dependence on fossil fuels imports, while taking into account the available natural resources (e.g., geological storage capacity, its geographical distribution, etc.), CCSU and carbon removals technological expectations and social acceptability concerns. In addition: • Under the Energy Efficiency Directive, energy efficiency must be treated as a primary energy source, with the Energy Efficiency First Principle guiding all policy, planning, and investment decisions through cost-benefit analysis and proper monitoring. • Each Member State should outline its carbon capture needs in its National Energy and Climate Plan and develop related transport and storage infrastructure accordingly. As carbon capture is a residual solution, EU-wide planning should be replaced by bilateral cooperation, with the European Commission facilitating. Operators opting for CCS or CCU must fund the infrastructure, which should be tailored to hard-to-abate sectors and scaled to match national needs and absorption capacity.

evidence.im_comment:
Strongly supporting the urgent decarbonization of the power sector. 
Supporting AEMO's Step Change scenario and advocating for all ISP 
scenarios to align with the 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement. Encouraging
 the Australian Government to identify and highlight policy gaps to ensure that 
existing policies, such as the expanded Capacity Investment Scheme, 
align with the pace of transition required (Iberdrola, comments on AEMO's Draft 2024 ISP, February 2024)
evidence.source_extract: Iberdrola welcomes the opportunity to make a submission on the Draft 2024 ISP. The Draft results highlight that significant action in both transmission and generation is required over the next decade to deliver the energy transition. This will require close collaboration between government, regulators, industry, and consumers to ensure that major projects can be delivered on time. To further the value of the ISP as a roadmap for the energy transition, AEMO should identify any areas where there is a misalignment between policy targets and existing policy mechanisms. This will help all governments to develop effective policy that minimises risk. We look forward to working closely with AEMO to accelerate projects that can deliver Australia’s climate goals. This will likely require projects beyond the currently proposed REZs and will require that there is willingness to engage with and support innovative projects and adapt to challenges in the pathway of the energy transition. [We broadly support the updates to scenario definition in the Draft 2024 ISP] It is critical that all scenarios for the ISP align with Australia’s commitments under the Paris Agreement to limit global temperature rises to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels. In particular, we note that the previous 2022 ISP’s adoption of the Step Change scenario as the ‘most likely’ scenario (as recommended by Iberdrola Australia) marks the first ISP which was not out of date within 12 months (as explicit policies caught up to climate commitments). Similarly, subsequent to finalisation of scenario assumptions for the 2024 ISP, the federal government announced their commitment to delivering 82% renewables through the Capacity Investment Scheme – consistent with the ISP assumptions. We therefore support AEMO in selecting scenarios that deliver a successful transition. [To ensure the effectiveness of the ISP as a roadmap, AEMO should clearly identify and highlight policy gaps in the transition] There is broad and deep agreement from all levels of government on the need to decarbonise the electricity system, which is reflected in the selection of scenarios in the Draft ISP. However, there can sometimes be misalignment between a policy target, and a credible well developed policy mechanism to achieve the target. The ISP is a valuable roadmap that illustrates a pathway to the energy transition. It demonstrates the need for investments in transmission capacity to support the optimal pathway, and highlights that government targets would be either be missed or that additional system costs would be incurred if transmission capacity is not developed. To further its value as a roadmap for the energy transition, it would be helpful for the ISP to clearly identify and articulate any policy ‘gaps’, where the successful achievement of existing policies does not align with the pace of transition required. For instance, where the achievement of any emissions reduction target or renewable energy target in AEMO’s modelling requires the implementation of a hard emissions constraint or other constraint that doesn’t reflect an existing legislated mechanism. If achieving government targets requires market intervention beyond existing government policies, this should be clearly articulated as part of the ISP. This would help guide the development of policies such as the expanded Capacity Investment Scheme and provide valuable guidance for where jurisdictions could effectively focus additional support to deliver the transition. This is particularly important over the current planning window, for projects under development to enter by 2030. We note that the ISP is a least-cost simulation rather than a price or investment forecast. As such, the ISP results should not be used to infer shortfalls in the energy market design. For example, the lack of committed long-duration storage projects in the market compared to the ISP modelling reflects a lack of certainty around the timing of coal closures not a failure of the energy only market (which has consistently delivered high levels of reliability and investment). Instead, gaps between ISP projections and currently announced investment commitments highlight the importance of implementing broad based emissions constraints in Australia, which could be further explored by AEMO. [Achieving the energy transition requires close collaboration between government, industry, and consumers] By considering scenarios that deliver a successful transition, the ISP provides a “roadmap” for the energy transition – that is, identifying the pace of change required and identifying major transmission infrastructure projects required on a forward-looking basis. While the required investment is a step up from historical levels, given Iberdrola’s understanding and experience in global supply chains, we consider Australia’s 82% renewable energy target is achievable by 2030 if projects are actioned quickly and AEMO and jurisdictions pursue all available opportunities. […] Further analysis of green fuels and electrification We consider that a focus area for future ISPs should be higher resolution modelling of electrification and green fuels (including hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol). This includes explicit modelling of green fuel storage, consideration of green fuel offtake requirements, and consideration of different pathways to electrification (including thermal energy storage). This could in turn affect the required generation mix and impact on electricity peak demand.

evidence.source_extract: The provisions of the US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) strongly support the development of cleantech and growing net zero aligned industries. It is also the most prominent recent example that shows how EU climate leadership has successfully catalysed a race to secure the benefits from the enormous economic opportunity that this deep transformation entails [...] GDIP is vital to speed up the transition to climate neutrality to ensure the EU delivers on its domestic climate objectives, and avoids a climate disaster. Energy security in Europe can only be guaranteed by accelerating clean solutions, reducing energy demand and phasing out fossil fuel consumption [...] The clear and stable EU energy and climate targets established for the short, medium and long-term must lead to sector goals and world-leading Single Market standards. evidence.source_extract: IBERDROLA welcomes the Proposal for a Regulation on a Union certification for carbon removals as a unique opportunity to set a proper regulatory framework for an EU-wide robust system to complement mitigation efforts and reach the net-zero ambitions. [...] While carbon removals will play an indispensable role in reaching EU’s climate neutrality goal for 2050, these should be primarily used for compensating for the residual CO2 emissions in hard-to-abate sectors, where no other solution is available. CO2 emissions abatement must remain the priority for EU regulations in the short and medium term, incentivising cost-effective and market-driven solutions (electrification, fossil fuels phasing out, deployment of renewables). [...] The voluntary basis incentivises the industrial uptake of high-quality carbon removals, in full respect of the biodiversity and the zero pollution objectives, and allows a period of adaptation of the industrial processes The 5 Mt industrial carbon removals target will contribute to not hindering the overriding mitigation solutions in the short term [...] Not considering fossil fuel sources in the carbon removal certification system is a good practice example of the “do not significant harm” principle that must be included in all the regulatory developments to avoid lock-in of fossil technologies

evidence.im_comment: Iberdrola supported the proposed eligibility criteria and for the inclusion of additionally measures, but appeared to not support the inclusion of mandatory temporal correlation. Iberdrola also appears to support the exclusion of certain end uses that do not deliver climate benefits such as coal-co firing and calls for the minimum 50 MW threshold to be raised (Iberdrola, comments on the Hydrogen Headstart Program, August 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Iberdrola Australia supports the restriction of the scheme to new, renewable hydrogen projects including zero emissions renewable hydrogen derivative projects (green ammonia, green methanol, green steel etc). [...] . 50 MW is likely to be low compared to scale required. We consider that the benefits of the program are likely to be maximised if it delivers commercial scale investments that can act as a template for future projects. [...] Time matching creates significant complexity and compliance costs for projects, requiring careful consideration of both generation and storage in supply. It can be voluntarily implemented by projects that require this (e.g., for export markets) but would be an unnecessary overhead for domestic supply at this time. In the near-term, every new renewable project will help offset coal generation (Nelson et al., 2022).We note that the vintage requirement on certificates will be important for ensuring that new loads lead to decarbonisation. For example, if existing renewables were used to supply a new load (without a corresponding increase in clean energy supply) it is likely that the energy balance would be delivered in the near-term by coal generation, leading to a net increase in emissions. [...] Given the early stage of the Australian industry, we broadly support allowing any end use. However, it would be reasonable to include a merit criteria that favours end uses that are likely to be part of the future generation mix. For example, Japan is considering co-firing of coal with ammonia. However, any use of thermal coal is not compatible with Australia’s commitments under the Paris Agreement. As such, indirect support of any project that doesn’t result in zero emissions might limit the long-term benefits of the government funding. [...] Australia’s economy, and therefore any hydrogen-related processes, will need close to zero actual emissions. It would be reasonable to require projects to be consistent with this long-term requirement.

evidence.im_comment: Supporting the EU Net Zero Industry Act with some technical conditions that do not seem to impact the overall ambition of the proposal. Stating that only the most efficient CSS projects should be developed and stressing that accepting large cost differences during renewable energy auctions will disincentivize electrification (Iberdrola, comments submitted on the EU Net Zero Industry Act, June 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Iberdrola supports the Commission initiative and objectives of the Net-zero Industry Act, as a globally balanced approach to facilitate the deployment of a European Union based industrial capacity bringing necessary resilience for the energy transition in Europe. However, Iberdrola has relevant objections as regards Articles 16, 18 and 20. Arts. 16-18: EU objective of CO2 injection capacity and contributions of oil gas producers All targets in EU legislation must be supported by impact assessments to evaluate their feasibility, their proportionality and their fitness to the objectives sought by the regulation […] None of this is found behind the target of 50 Mt of CO2 injection capacity by 2030, in comparison to max. 75-300 Mt annual injection capacity needs expected by the Commission by 2050. […] Once an impact assessment has defined the most cost-effective pathway to net-zero, considering the relative contribution of carbon removals and the different technological and regulatory tools to deploy, only the most efficient CO2 injection projects should be developed across de EU and not those getting more support from local Member States. In addition, the contribution of authorised oil and gas producers to the EU CO2 injection objective shall be considered an expression of the polluters pay principle. […] Art. 20 Auctions to deploy renewable energy sources Achieving 2030 EU decarbonisation targets and climate neutrality by 2050 links to massive investment in assets to produce new renewable energy, which is the main driver for facilitating these objectives in the most efficient way. The introduction of well-defined and transparent sustainability and resilience criteria in auctions to deploy new renewable can bring support to EU industry with whole compliance with market and efficiency principles and facilitate a more balanced approach to tenders than purely based on prices. However, accepting costs differences on market standards (up to 10%, according to the Commission proposal) is a flagrant breach of market and efficiency principles. Imposing the cost difference has consequences on the relative prices of the energy drivers, making electricity more expensive vs. other energies (fossil). This hampers the electrification of the economy and in consequence, the pathway towards an effective and efficient decarbonisation.

evidence.im_comment: Supporting carbon removals in the EU 2040 Target for the residual CO2 emissions in hard-to-abate sectors and acknowledging the need to prioritize GHG emissions reductions. Stating that decarbonization efforts should be driven primarily by direct electrification based on renewable energy (Iberdrola, comments submitted on EU climate target for 2040, June 2023)
evidence.source_extract: The energy transition requires important efforts from all sectors. An efficient decarbonisation requires that carbon emissions abatement (mitigation effort) remains the priority for EU in the short and medium term, incentivising cost-effective and market-driven solutions (electrification, fossil fuels phasing out, deployment of renewables). In those hard-to-abate sectors where mitigation is difficult due to lack of low-cost commercially available mitigation or implementation challenges, carbon removals can play a role. […] 1) Direct electrification based on renewable energy must be the main pillar of decarbonization as the only “no-regret” option and the most effective way to decarbonise most of the economy. 2) Other renewable alternatives, as renewable hydrogen and derivatives or sustainable biofuels, must be targeted in end-use sectors where there are no other efficient alternatives (i.e. “hard-to-abate industry, maritime transport or aviation”). 3) Carbon removals will play a role in reaching EU’s climate neutrality goal for 2050: these should be primarily used for neutralizing for the residual CO2 emissions in hard-to-abate sectors, where no other solution is available.

evidence.im_comment: Evidence suggests advocating for renewable hydrogen measures in Australia's National Hydrogen Strategy, specifying the need to prioritize hard-to-abate sectors. Entity is promoting need for long-term investment signals and a hydrogen production credit scheme to support the development of hydrogen in Australia, however without stating the need to increase renewable energy capacity overall. Entity also appears to support the immediate replacement of fossil fuel exports with hydrogen and hydrogen derivatives and the introduction of hydrogen production targets, though emphasizes the need for further analysis (Iberdrola Australia, comments on DCCEEW's Review of the National Hydrogen Strategy, August 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Iberdrola Australia is committed to the decarbonising of the Australian economy. The electricity sector has a critical role to play, both through being the “low hanging fruit” of emissions reduction and through the direct or indirect electrification of other sectors. Green hydrogen and derivatives provide a critical intermediary fuel that can help leverage Australia’s low-cost electricity to decarbonise (both onshore and offshore) and create new local jobs and growth opportunities. […] The Hydrogen Headstart program has the potential to kickstart investment in Australian hydrogen production, and associated downstream use cases. However, it only targets up to 1 GW of electrolysers. There will likely be an opportunity to bring projects to market that are unsuccessful in the Hydrogen Headstart program (e.g., due to not being sufficiently progressed) if there is an ongoing signal. [...] A long-term signal for investment in hydrogen will help avoid “boom and bust” cycles of hydrogen or cliff edges where investment drops off. [...] We also see significant opportunities for hydrogen to create new industries and growth opportunities in Australia. This includes directly at production facilities, or indirectly through new green steel or manufacturing opportunities. [...] Complementing a national fungible carbon scheme, we also consider the government should consider complementary short- and medium-term policies that will induce hydrogen demand, help bring the industry down the cost curve faster, and facilitate the development of dependent industries. For example, a local hydrogen industry could enhance our balance of trade either directly by facilitating hydrogen exports or indirectly by onshoring processes such as green steel. [...] Hydrogen specific options could include an ongoing production credit scheme that would capture the national economic benefits of domestic hydrogen production. The government could potentially focus on a scheme where the value of production credits falls over time to encourage continued cost reductions (similar to how the total STCs for rooftop solar PV systems have declined over time). Alternatively, national, state, or sectoral production targets could be implemented to meet strategic goals (e.g., installed electrolyser capacity, volume of hydrogen, volume of methanol or green steel, etc.). However, with the industry still in the early stages and pathways to commercialisation still being explored and developed, significant further analysis will be required before realistic targets can be developed. [...] The key sectors for targeting will be those that cannot be directly electrified, or where the sector provides a strategic opportunity to invest in Australia’s future. This includes using or supporting retraining of existing workforces in new sectors. We also note that existing fossil fuel exports are c$100bn p.a. in value; these exports are not consistent with Australia’s commitments under the Paris Agreement. Alternative exports need to be identified and progressed immediately. Hydrogen and hydrogen derivatives are a key opportunity in this context. [...] Key sectors where hydrogen appears to be particularly valuable include: •Chemicals, particularly ammonia and methanol (for use in industrial processes, as well as alternative liquid fuels); •Low emissions metals, particularly iron and alumina; • High temperature process heating; • Electricity firming, either directly as hydrogen or through liquid fuels. In contrast, hydrogen for transport currently appears to be a relatively niche product, where direct electrification is preferable.

evidence.im_comment: Supporting capacity mechanisms with stricter criteria to avoid fossil fuel lock in, but also appearing to not support explicit measures to scale up demand response, stating that demand response, generation and energy storage should be incentivized equally (Iberdrola, comments submitted on Electricity market – reform of the EU’s electricity market design, February 2023)
evidence.source_extract: [Do you consider appropriate to enable a product to foster demand reduction and shift energy at peak times as an ancillary service, aiming at lowering fuel consumption and reducing the prices?] No [Do you have additional comments?] Flexibility with explicit demand response has a lot of potential, but its use is limited if we don´t want to affect to economy. The consumption of electricity is necessary to produce goods and services with added value for society. Moreover, consumers have the essential right “to consume” at the time and in the form they want/need. Conversely, generation and storage assets are fit and ready to serve the electricity system at any time and hence, to give a service to consumers. [...] Therefore, for the sake of efficiency and level playing field, we need to guarantee that there are no other resources (generation, storage) in the power system that can provide the same value for money or less compared to explicit DSR. [Do you consider the current setup for capacity mechanisms adequate to respond to the investment needs as regards firm capacity, in particular to better support the uptake of storage and demand side response?] Yes [Do you have additional comments?] Capacity remuneration mechanisms provide signals to invest in the resources needed to meet the long-term reliability standard (i.e., generation, storage, demand-side response) consistent with the decarbonisation and energy-independence targets. Define tighter eligibility criteria for new capacities to effectively avoid fossil energy / carbon lock-ins. Such criteria should be progressively increased under a clearly defined ex-ante path, with no grandfathering clause. Consistently with the energy-independence target, new and existing fossil capacities should have a limited load factor as a precondition for participation in the capacity market. Make auction lead-time and contract duration long enough for technologies key for decarbonisation to be able to participate in the capacity mechanism, particularly long-duration storage (e.g., pumped storage).

evidence.im_comment: Supporting clean hydrogen with major exceptions: emphasizing concerns with incorporating hourly time-matching into the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean hydrogen tax credit. Hourly matching would require hydrogen to be produced in the same hours when renewable energy is being generated, whereas annual matching would allow hydrogen facilities to claim the tax credit even when they produce clean hydrogen for only a portion of the taxable year (Joint letter to policymakers, April 2023)
evidence.source_extract: The 45V Production Tax Credit (PTC) for clean hydrogen has the potential to accelerate the decarbonization of numerous sectors, including agriculture, heavy industry, maritime shipping, long-haul road transport, aviation, and the power sector. We write to urge you to implement the pragmatic policies needed to achieve the PTC’s goal to establish an affordable clean hydrogen economy across the United States. [...] Specifically, we support the use of “annual matching” for hydrogen producers to qualify for the section 45V tax credit. Under annual matching, renewable power generation is matched to the electricity consumed for hydrogen production on an annual basis. With only 12.4% of U.S. primary energy consumption coming from renewables, annual matching is an effective method to jumpstart the clean hydrogen economy in a climate-responsible way. By replacing high-carbon-intensity fuels in downstream applications, hydrogen produced through annual matching can be both clean and cost effective. In contrast, hourly matching would increase the price of clean hydrogen to effectively negate the economic and decarbonization benefits of the hydrogen PTC. [...] The clean hydrogen that will be produced as a result of pragmatic implementation of section 45V will have tremendous climate benefits. The use of clean hydrogen to replace diesel fuel, kerosene, marine bunker fuel, and pet coke will help to displace significant quantities of carbon dioxide emissions and other harmful pollutants, such as sulfur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter. Annual matching will deliver these substantial benefits, especially to traditionally underserved and disadvantaged communities that have been disproportionately affected, helping to achieve the environmental justice goals of the Biden administration. These downstream benefits have been overlooked by advocates of more restrictive temporal matching. [...] By offsetting the benefit of the PTC, hourly matching would severely affect the number of jobs supporting green hydrogen. Investments in electrolyzer manufacturing and innovation would be disincentivized, and the U.S. would lose the opportunity to be a global hydrogen production leader. In fact, recent studies warn that overly stringent temporal matching would hinder the development of the clean hydrogen industry, holding back its critical role in long-term decarbonization of the U.S. economy.

evidence.source_extract: Avangrid commends BOEM’s decision to allow other critical activities – infrastructure developments such as ports upgrades related to component manufacturing and supply chain elements necessary for green hydrogen generation - to qualify for the bidding credit.

evidence.im_comment:
Evidence suggests advocating for more ambitious building electrification measures: subsidiary Berkshire Gas Company appearing to advocate to Massachusetts policymakers to design a Clean Heat Standard that incentivizes electrification and financially discourages fossil fuel heating (Mass Save Program Administrators’ Joint Comments on Clean Heat Standard 
Discussion Document, Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection, December 2023)
evidence.source_extract: The Draft Regulatory Framework’s proposal to impose a compliance obligation on all forms of heating fuels, including electricity, would serve to increase the cost of electricity and deter customers from adopting heat pumps. Instead, to create meaningful incentives for customers, the CHS needs to raise the cost of GHG-intensive fuels, such as oil and propane, relative to electricity. A policy as simple as assessing a surcharge on fossil fuels with revenues directed towards electrification, with all or most revenues dedicated to low- and moderate-income (“LMI”) customers, would fill these regulatory gaps and satisfy DEP’s broad and flexible direction from the Clean Heat Commission. [...] the PAs are concerned that the Draft Regulatory Framework’s proposal to require compliance by demonstrating both clean heat installations (through “full electrification credits”) and ongoing operation (through “emission reduction credits”) is unnecessarily complex. For customers who already have access to Mass Save rebates, the full electrification credit proposal would create customer confusion and complicate the decisions for customers, installers, and fuel providers. For example, although we appreciate the intent of assigning Clean Heat Credits to customers in the first instance, realistically, this will lead to disputes among installers, obligated entities, and the PAs over who will contract with customers to acquire Clean Heat Credits.

evidence.im_comment: Evidence suggests supporting specific building electrification measures with major exceptions: subsidiary Berkshire Gas Company appearing to advocate to Massachusetts policymakers to design a flexible Clean Heat Standard that includes a long-term role for "gas-fired components" and "clean heat fuels", without clearly defining these fuels (Mass Save Program Administrators’ Joint Comments on Clean Heat Standard Discussion Document, Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection, May 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Increasingly, the Mass Save program is evolving into an electrification and decarbonization program, with a particular focus during the current 2022-24 term on electrifying heating through the deployment of air source heat pumps. [...] An effective Clean Heat Standard should integrate seamlessly with the existing Mass Save program. It should support both the further deployment of demand-reducing measures like weatherization and the electrification of heat, and it should encourage the optimal use of heating systems, including those that continue to include gas-fired components. An effective Clean Heat Standard should leverage the progress the PAs have made thus far in transforming the market for heat pumps, particularly building the contractor workforce to deploy these systems. [...] Green hydrogen could be an instrumental tool in decarbonizing difficult-to-electrify industry sectors. Whether used in energy storage applications, fuel cells, or for combustion, hydrogen is a zero-carbon fuel ideally positioned to support local, state, and federal decarbonization goals. Developing a robust green hydrogen economy may additionally support the expansion of renewable energy generation, helping to mitigate variation in production and providing a demand for curtailed energy. Hydrogen blending into natural gas infrastructure can reduce end-use emissions associated with natural gas, decarbonizing difficult-to-electrify customers across the Avangrid CT network. Additionally, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles are an ideal complement to electric vehicles, with applications for light, medium, and especially heavy-duty vehicles. Vehicles may be served by gaseous or liquid hydrogen, providing a zero-carbon, energy-dense fuel that is not negatively impacted by cold weather like EVs. Green hydrogen can be used to produce other synthetic fuels like ammonia and methanol for vehicle and vessel decarbonization. With the price of fossil-based ammonia (gray ammonia) at an all-time high, green ammonia can provide a cleaner and cost competitive option to develop and expand local and regional fertilizer industry. [...] It should be noted that the technology breakthrough and economy of scale in electrolyzer manufacturing, along with the growth of renewable energy resources such as onshore/offshore wind and solar projects, will significantly reduce the levelized cost of green hydrogen production within the next few decades. Hydrogen produced by SMR and CG does generate GHG byproducts, and as a result must employ extensive Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Sequestration (“CCUS”) technology at the production site in order to reduce GHG emission. Even when CCUS is included in SMR and CG production, it cannot capture all GHG emission through the hydrogen production process, let alone the significant amounts of GHGs emitted upstream in the process to source the natural and coal feedstocks required. Regardless of the method of hydrogen production, it is essential to locate production facilities as close to offtakers as possible, reducing the cost of transportation and distribution.

evidence.source_extract: As companies and organizations committed to building America’s clean energy future, we write to request that Fiscal Year 2023 Energy and Water Appropriations provide robust funding for high-voltage transmission deployment and research through the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Grid Deployment Office, Loan Programs Office (LPO), and Office of Electricity (OE). Our energy transmission infrastructure is essential to providing Americans access to the power they need. To ensure American families and businesses always have access to power, it is imperative that we invest in and build new transmission to make our grid more reliable, resilient, and interconnected. Upgraded and expanded transmission lines will keep costs down by bringing diverse types of affordable, clean power to more communities. Additionally, the expansion and modernization of our national power grid is central to meeting our nation’s urgent climate and energy security goals. Congress took critical first steps to meeting these goals in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) by investing $2.5 billion in direct spending for new transmission and expanding programs aimed at enhancing our grid resilience. However, more will be necessary going forward. Some estimates suggest that fully decarbonizing our electric grid will require high-voltage transmission capacity to expand by 60 percent by 2030, and to triple by 2050. More limited capacity for MSs to apply exemptions and reductions. • Obligation to every MS to keep the ranking established in the tax scale for each use in the national transposition. • Recognition of environmental performance of electricity through minimal tax rates and the environmental low performance of all fossil liquid and gaseous energy vectors. In addition, certain aspects of this proposal could be further improved: • Excessively long transition period (10 years) to adapt minimum rates of fossil or not fully sustainable energies. It does not seem to be justified to freeze minimum rates during the whole transition period for the so called “low carbon” energies. The concept of “low carbon” energy is itself ambiguous as far as linked to Taxonomy legislation expected to be regularly updated (e.g. could consumers/producers of “low carbon” energies get a kind of grandfathering if taxonomy changes the definition of “low carbon”?). • Incentives to best performing energies in air and waterborne transport are not applied to road mobility. • The whole of “renewable fuels of non-biological origin” (essentially renewable hydrogen and its synthetic derivatives) are treated the same, while the environmental performance (efficiency in production and use) is radically different among them. evidence.im_comment: Supporting EU's Energy System Integration and Hydrogen Strategy, and advocating for renewable hydrogen to be prioritized (Joint Letter to Frans Timmermans - Executive Vice-President of the European Commission, Kadri Simson - European Commissioner for Energy, and Thierry Breton - European Commissioner for the Internal Market on Renewable Hydrogen in the EU Hydrogen Strategy, July 2020)
evidence.source_extract: Amidst the COVID-19 health and economic crises, Europe needs to prioritise the most efficient, sustainable and cost-effective pathways to decarbonise its economy. In the past years renewables such as wind and solar have become the most affordable energy sources, accelerating the decarbonisation of the power sector and creating long-term jobs for over 400,000 Europeans. Renewables provide a proven and scalable solution to achieve full decarbonisation. More than 60% of final energy consumption can be covered by direct electrification of final energy uses, such as road transport, heating and buildings, and industrial processes, with an energy system based on renewables. The upcoming Energy System Integration Strategy must accelerate the deployment of renewable electricity across these sectors, modernising Europe’s electricity grid infrastructure and driving the electrification of the economy. The potential of renewables in Europe remains largely untapped. The sustained deployment of renewables will enable the production of CO2 free and cost-competitive renewable hydrogen - making fossil-based alternatives redundant. Produced through electrolysis and with 100% renewable electricity, renewable hydrogen is the key to bringing forward the competitive decarbonisation of those sectors difficult to electrify, such as energy intensive industries, aviation and shipping. All while enhancing our energy security and helping balance our energy system. The upcoming EU Hydrogen Strategy must build on our flourishing renewables industry to develop a robust and competitive EU electrolyser industry. Together, the renewables, storage and electrolyser industries can be the bedrock of Europe’s energy sector employing millions of Europeans by 2050. But investors need clear guidance and visibility. The EU renewable hydrogen success story can only be achieved by enacting a clear commitment towards renewable hydrogen as the only “Clean hydrogen”. As the one pathway compatible with climate neutrality, renewable hydrogen must be the focus of market pull measures, industrial up-scaling and R&D - notably in the frame of the EU Clean Hydrogen Alliance

evidence.im_comment: Opposing policies which aid the decarbonization of the economy: directly advocating to policymakers to oppose Connecticut House Bill 5350 on limiting the expansion of fossil gas infrastructure in the state (Avangrid, Testimony on House Bill 5350 - An Act Concerning Natural Gas Infrastructure, Connecticut Energy and Technology Committee, March 2020)
evidence.source_extract: We support the provisions of the Bill that would advance Connecticut the generation of locally generated renewable gas. We also support the provisions that would order steps to improve the condition of the gas distribution systems to reduce the leakage from those systems. Despite our support for those aspects of the Bill, we are opposed to Raised Bill 5530 because of the provisions in Section 2 that would limit customer’s access to natural gas service. Section 2 of Raised Bill would change the “hurdle rate”, which in turn would increase the contribution a customer has to make to connect to the natural gas system. While some might say that this step is necessary to combat climate change and encourage customers to instead choose heat pumps, we believe that taking this step today is not sound public policy that would result in reduced carbon emissions but rather would increase carbon emissions for the foreseeable future. [...] While natural gas is still a carbon based fuel, and still emits greenhouse gases when burned, it is significantly better than other fossil fuels we might use. Access to natural gas is also an important economic development tool for the state of Connecticut. Natural gas remains 25-30% less expensive than alternative higher carbon fuels. This translates to savings for customers who can then use that savings to help spur the Connecticut economy. Access to lower cost natural gas is also an economic imperative for our businesses to maintain their competitive position relative to other lower cost energy states. In addition to a lower cost choice, some businesses may not be able to meet their industrial process needs with heat pump technologies available today, forcing them to use higher carbon fuels if they don’t have access to natural gas.

evidence.im_comment: Directly advocating for policy, infrastructure and investments or other systems that aid the development of hydrogen produced using renewable energy, while also supporting additional renewable energy capacity to support this (Iberdrola, Comments on EU Hydrogen Strategy, June 2020)
evidence.source_extract: Although green H2 is called to be a relevant energy carrier in the decarbonisation, it is still immature, with low energy efficiency and presents limitations in terms of production and transport. Its current cost is more than double the cost of RES-E and its future still depends on solving the technological uncertainties of H2. Energy Sector Integration is intended to be the EU’s tool to ensure decarbonisation is achieved at the lowest possible cost, which should optimise the use of RES-E as the main energy carrier for decarbonisation along with other carbon neutral options in those niche sectors where electrification is not yet possible. The EU’s H2 Strategy should take into consideration all these circumstances and establish an adequate framework for its development, avoiding a massive implementation too early and making sure that it is consistent with the decarbonisation strategy. Iberdrola believes that this strategy should: a) Guarantee that H2 is green, from 100% renewable electricity and has no carbon footprint. Considering that the EU must be carbon neutral by 2050, it is not consistent to use grey or blue H2 as they originate from fossil fuels and emit CO2. These alternatives should not even be used as a transitory measure to kick off a future green H2 market. A robust certification system will be required to ensure this (the current GO system is not appropriate due to its lack of geographical and locational correlation) and the additionality principle of the RED2 must be respected. b) Preserve the technology neutrality principle and guarantee a level playing field between the decarbonised energy carriers, in order to promote competition and efficient end uses at the lowest possible cost. • Set energy and climate objectives (emissions reduction, renewables and energy efficiency) to meet EU’s long term decarbonisation objectives. Sub-objectives for each energy carrier should not be established, as this would encourage their development regardless of their technological maturity • The carbon leakage industry must be protected and, at the same time, it must be ensured that it contributes to decarbonisation. The industry that produces grey H2 currently receives free carbon allowances, leaving green H2 at a competitive disadvantage. In this context, a Carbon Border Tax or Adjustment at EU level is required • All investments must be supported by a CBA that internalises all costs. i.e. for a blue H2 plant, account should be taken not only the cost of H2 production, but also the cost of transporting and storing CO2, the investment needed to adapt the current gas grid and the stranded costs involved as these assets cannot be used beyond 2050) c) Promote efficient decarbonisation using green H2 in those final uses where it has most value: • Promote the technological development of green H2 in demonstration projects to improve its maturity and competitiveness with R&D grants from European funds • Ensure that possible support schemes for RES-E used to produce green H2 are included in the general renewable framework. evidence.source_extract: Now, our energy outlook actually -- not by necessarily taking those models, but just by our own work, would indicate that we're somewhere in kind of in the middle of where those models are. The policy choices of controlling the temperature rise to 2 degrees centigrade, tend to require you to operate on the lower boundary of those models which is extremely challenging to achieve which is why we said you need to be thinking about plan B. But my response here with everyone needing to understand, we don't really know what the climate effects of 600 ppm versus 450 ppm will be, because the models simply are not that good. Having said that, we strongly support and have supported continued scientific investigation, continued perfection of the models, and they will get better. We're collecting so much more data today than we were 10 years ago. We have high speed computing available to use today that we did not have 10 years ago. So we anticipate, we hope, that the [confidence] of the models begin to close and therefore you can have a higher confidence around the outcome. So I would preface my answer with, I don't want to suggest that we know at 650, you get x-centimeters rise in sea level versus 450 because the models just aren't that good. But it is a risk management problem which we have always described it. And in risk management, you have to consider the range of possible consequences and be prepared for those. So that's why we have always posed this question of what if everything we do, it turns out our models were really lousy and we achieved all our objectives, but it turned out the planet behaved differently because the models just weren't good enough to predict. What's plan B? Our plan B has always been grounded in our beliefs around the continued evolution of technology and engineered solutions to address and react to whatever the climate system and its outcomes present to us, whether that be in the form of rises in sea level which we think you can address through different engineering accommodations along coastal areas, to changing agricultural production due to changes in weather patterns that may or may not be induced by climate change. And we believe there are today a number of studies and efforts underway not just with academic but at also private institutions beginning to think about the implications of that. And how can our economic system, and I use that in its broadest terms, from the food we eat to the water we consume, to how we produce, the products that provide us with -- how does it adjust to the climate that's moving around it, and what our belief without giving you a long [laundry] list, is that we are highly confident, because we're a science and engineering company, because you see a lot of technologies that we have developed and people in our industry developed, and people in other industries are developing, that mankind has this enormous capacity to deal with adversity and that there are -- those solutions will present themselves as the realities become clear either through improved modeling and (inaudible) the predictive capabilities of the models or as they are evidenced to us. (Rex Tillerson 'Annual Shareholder Meeting, May 27 2015', Fair Disclosure Wire)

Failing to do so could prompt companies like ExxonMobil to rethink their commitment to the region. evidence.source_extract: The ExxonMobil view is that the Circular Economy is one with a systematic approach to resource management to reduce, reuse or recover the use or value of a product before it becomes a waste. [...] To unlock the full value of waste—specifically end-of-life plastics—as a resource, decisive legislative action is needed. The European Commission can support this by harmonizing end-of-waste criteria, strengthening controls to protect the integrity of plastic recyclates, streamlining permitting processes, and ensuring consistent Extended Producer Responsibility rules across member states. [...] Both mechanical and chemical recycling (e.g., depolymerization, gasification, pyrolysis) are essential, each suited to specific material types and end-uses. Europe needs all recycling approaches to build a resilient and inclusive circular economy for all these plastics. [...] Mechanical recycling plays a key role in Europe’s circularity goals, offering a cost-effective model that supports EU regulations like the Single Use Plastics Directive and the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation. However, for contact-sensitive uses or hard-to-recycle plastics, alternative technologies are also needed to scale circularity. There is no single chemical recycling technology that fits all needs. Pyrolysis is essential for processing hard-to-recycle plastics made from polyolefins. Depolymerization technologies—used for certain plastics like PET—do not work for breaking down polyolefins. These technologies are therefore critical to meeting Europe’s circularity objectives: delivering the same value as mechanical recycling in reducing waste to incineration, and by replacing virgin raw materials. [...] For industry to monetize their investments, all outputs coming from the processing of end-of-life plastics should be entitled to generate a recycled content premium, which must be attributed where market demand exists, notably in circular polymers. [...] For recovered plastics feedstock to play a greater role in the circular economy, a clear definition of the status of secondary raw materials is needed. We strongly believe the best path to preserve good auto jobs and keep new vehicles affordable for more Americans is a final rule supported by all parties—including California. Such a final rule would provide the necessary structure and compliance tools to achieve annual fuel economy improvements midway between the existing standards and the preferred path outlined by your Administration last summer. The final rule would cover model years 2021-2026 and include flexibilities that promote advanced technology for the sake of long-term environmental gains and U.S. global competitiveness. We encourage both the federal government and California to resume discussions and to remain open to regulatory adjustments that provide the flexibility needed to meet future environmental goals and respond to consumer needs.

evidence.source_extract: I would like to report on Toyota Motor Corporation’s initiatives regarding hydrogen. Please turn to page 1. First, although this may be stating the obvious, I would like to take this opportunity to briefly review what hydrogen is. We believe that hydrogen is a future energy source that can be produced domestically using electricity—primarily from renewable energy—and water. Hydrogen can be utilized not only in mobility but also across a wide range of industries, including power generation, the chemical industry, and steelmaking. Furthermore, we believe it is possible to expand its applications even further into general-purpose uses, as it can replace natural gas through processes such as methanation. There are certain areas where it is difficult to achieve full replacement with electricity. As an energy source capable of replacing fossil fuels in these areas, we do not view this as a choice between “electricity or hydrogen”; rather, we believe both electricity and hydrogen will be essential for Japan’s future. Furthermore, as mentioned earlier, regarding the social infrastructure aspects of the value chain—namely, production, transportation, and storage—while these are becoming established through the application of existing technologies, we believe it is crucial to invest in infrastructure with a focus on national-level efficiency. Within this context, regarding the “use” segment, the cost gap for replacing existing fuels is the smallest. Furthermore, there is a growing expectation among stakeholders that we should lead the societal implementation of hydrogen through mobility—a sector where the entire supply chain, encompassing production, transportation, and use, has already been commercialized. Please turn to page 2. There are challenges involved in introducing hydrogen mobility. We are very grateful that the government has already announced policies for the societal implementation of hydrogen mobility. I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude once again. To achieve a sustainable mobility model, the planned and large-scale consumption of hydrogen by commercial vehicles is key. Taking Heiwajima in Tokyo as an example, by introducing 80 commercial vehicles—including 40 large trucks—we have begun to see prospects for achieving hydrogen prices on par with existing fuels, albeit with some public support. We intend to use this as the foundation for a sustainable success model and ensure its implementation in each of the priority regions designated by the government. Furthermore, by connecting these regions via major arterial roads, we aim to create a hydrogen highway that spans the length of Japan. For many years, we have faced what is often referred to as the “chicken-and-egg problem,” but I believe the time has finally come when we can break free from this dilemma. I sincerely hope to achieve this through a united effort between the public and private sectors. Let me now turn my attention briefly to the international stage. […] If hydrogen is incorporated into the growth strategy, I believe the private sector will be able to accelerate its progress. Furthermore, I believe we are standing at a critical crossroads: if we halt the momentum of hydrogen-related initiatives now, Japan’s competitiveness 30 years from now will be significantly altered. I strongly urge you to position hydrogen as a strategic national investment area, and I hope that through public-private collaboration, we can contribute to strengthening Japan’s long-term competitiveness. Furthermore, particularly in the mobility sector, Toyota will lead technological development and make a substantial contribution to market formation. To address this across industries, we will collaborate with the Hydrogen Value Chain Promotion Council and work together with government officials to tackle challenges at the national level.

evidence.im_comment: Advocating for the use of hydrogen in light and heavy-duty vehicles to compliment electrification; claiming that current regulation is overly strict; statement takes no clear position on the need to decarbonize hydrogen production (Joint letter to policymakers, January 2025)
evidence.source_extract: Given the importance of the automotive industry for the European economy, its impact on employment, and the eroding competitiveness of the sector mentioned in the Draghi report, the undersigned companies urge the Commission to recognise the relevance of hydrogen mobility for the future of the automotive sector. We are convinced that hydrogen will play a crucial role in decarbonizing mobility, while improving the competitiveness of the sector and building a more resilient energy system in Europe. Over the years, vehicle manufacturers, suppliers, and infrastructure companies have made significant investments in Europe to gain a competitive advantage in hydrogen mobility. This has been done as a way to offer consumers a complementary solution to other zero emission vehicle (ZEV) alternatives, such as battery electric vehicles (BEV). However, misalignment between industry and policy makers, coupled with an overly strict regulatory framework has slowed down the hydrogen mobility market, putting the scale-up and the competitiveness of the industry strongly at risk. Therefore, the undersigned companies urge the Commission to include hydrogen mobility in the agenda for the Strategic Dialogue In contrast to battery electric technology, which is a needed solution to achieve decarbonization but where Europe lags foreign competition, when it comes to hydrogen mobility, Europe still has a chance of staying ahead not only on technological expertise and industrial capacity, but also on the needed supply chain, all of which are already present in Europe today. This is exactly why the European Union, its member states, and industry have already invested billions of euros in the deployment of hydrogen vehicles and their related refueling infrastructure. This includes significant European funds directed to IPCEI (Important Projects of Common European Interest) projects, national funding schemes, and private investment. [...] We therefore request that hydrogen mobility be an integral part of the upcoming Strategic Dialogue. Not only is hydrogen an answer to the decarbonization of heavy-duty vehicles, but also a needed complementary solution to battery electric vehicles when it comes to passenger cars and vans. It offers European consumers a wider range of options to address their particular decarbonization needs [...] Pursuing multiple technological solutions to address the decarbonization of transport only increases the chances of European industry becoming more competitive. This element is rightly emphasized in the Draghi report, and is an approach widely followed in China today, with the difference that when it comes to hydrogen mobility, Europe still holds a global competitive advantage. Additionally, the needed technology, supply chain, and industrial capacity can all be based in Europe. This is true from a vehicle perspective and its components, as well as the hydrogen needed to fuel them and related infrastructure, all of which are recognized by current EU funding and regulations. The need to create resilient and competitive supply chains should not be forgotten in the political debate.

evidence.im_comment: Opposing government policies that promote the sale of electric vehicles in the US. evidence.source_extract: Toyota Motor North America, Inc. (Toyota) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) referenced above. As a member of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (AAI), Toyota supports and incorporates by reference the AAI’s comments. [...] Toyota believes that any future vehicle emissions standards should be performance-based and promote the continued innovation of cleaner, more efficient vehicles while assuring consumers have the choice of products they want and can afford. Further, EPA should return to treating fuels and vehicles as a holistic system and consider regulations to compel advanced, lower-carbon liquid fuels in the market. Regardless of the pace of electrification of the nation’s fleet, legacy vehicles operating on gasoline will constitute a significant portion of the in-use fleet for decades to come and present a huge opportunity for emissions reductions. Finally, EPA should consider a regulatory structure that incorporates emissions upstream of the tailpipe as a more appropriate and balanced approach for capturing the performance of various powertrains. At a minimum, the standards-setting process needs a more complete and accurate assessment of the full emissions profile of competing powertrains. [...] In short, the GHG and criteria pollutant standards in the Multipollutant Final Rule combine to form a back-door electric vehicle (EV) mandate at levels Toyota believes are not feasible in today’s market. For example, by 2032 MY, the light-duty GHG standards project a 70% EV market share, while the light-duty Tier 4 NMOG+NOx fleet average standards are predicated on 50% EV share. Today’s 9.5% EV market share must triple by 2027 MY and grow seven-fold by 2032 MY to meet EPA’s projected range assumed for compliance. Such aggressive growth is extremely unlikely and is further challenged by the elimination of various EV tax credits upon which the Multipollutant Final Rule heavily relied. Further, a nascent battery supply chain, lack of charging infrastructure, and insufficient consumer demand limit the near-to-mid-term market outlook for EVs. The Multipollutant Final Rule fails to demonstrate how these challenges – many of which are outside the direct control of auto manufacturers – can be overcome in time to support the required levels of electrification.
