evidence.im_comment: Not supporting mandatory targets to decarbonize corporate fleets, while supporting incentives; emphasizing concerns including economic pressure and competitiveness (Joint letter to President Ursula von der Leyen, December 2025)
evidence.source_extract: We are writing to express our deep concern that a European Commission proposal requiring the mandatory purchase of Zero Emission Vehicles, either through national or European targets, will act as a further drag on the competitiveness of companies in Europe. At stake is the European automotive industry [...] companies are leading the switch to electric vehicles in Europe, more so than individual vehicle owners. Each of us has demonstrated a commitment to move to cleaner mobility as fast as the incentive frameworks and enabling conditions allow. The main obstacles for the acceleration of the uptake of ZEVs is a combination of managing the fleet Total Cost of Ownership paired with a lack of sufficient charging infrastructure suitable to all corporate use cases, for passenger and light commercial vehicles throughout Europe, and consequently a growing but still too slow demand from consumers. This is compounded by grid capacity and infrastructure permitting issues [...] We respectfully and urgently request that you focus on the powers and the resources of the Commission, working closely with the Member States, on the removal of these obstacles that will greatly help accelerate corporate ZEV uptake in Europe. An obligation to procure a mandatory share of zero-emission vehicles as part of the automotive package to be presented in December, would be highly damaging. Procuring ZEVs at the levels frequently suggested, would be financially crippling and leave companies with one of two choices, possibly both: retaining older vehicles for longer and/or reducing new vehicle purchases [...] The clear lessons of the European countries with the fastest ZEV uptake is that a combination of comprehensive incentive measures and investment in enabling conditions over a sustained period of time is the recipe for success. None of these countries have resorted to purchase mandates. Adequately incentivizing the uptake of second-hand ZEVs is absolutely essential to address massive over-supply and to stimulate new vehicle demand [...] We respectfully ask that you reconsider the adoption of this proposal and instead work with Member States and companies to replicate the best practices and investment in enabling conditions that will enable us to sustainably green our fleets faster – across all EU Member States.

evidence.im_comment: Opposing mandatory targets to decarbonize corporate fleets. Advocating for technology-neutrality over the complete electrification of road transport in the EU (Toyota Motor, Response to EU Consultation on Clean Corporate Vehicles, September 2025)
evidence.source_extract: Toyota appreciates that the Commission acknowledges zero-emissions vehicles (ZEV) demand for Passenger Cars (PC) and Light Commercial Vehicles (LCV) in Europe remains below required levels. However, introducing a mandate for corporate fleets would be counterproductive. It risks collapsing residual values, increasing total cost of ownership, and slowing fleet renewal—especially in markets lacking infrastructure or incentives. This would reduce affordability, delay purchases, and shrink demand, ultimately harming consumers, fleet operators, and the automotive value chain. [...] A more effective approach is to strengthen enabling conditions—such as charging infrastructure, fiscal incentives, and regulatory consistency—allowing market-driven uptake and preserving competitiveness across diverse fleet types and Member States. [...] Mandates targeting large fleets risk unintended consequences for SMEs and individuals, who often lease vehicles to companies falling under such rules. Similarly, private demand for short-term rental of ZEV is notoriously low and rental companies cannot force their customers to take ZEVs. Rental car companies represent a significant share of total fleet sales of OEMs. A uniform ZEV mandate risks penalising companies in regions with limited infrastructure or in sectors where electric options remain technically or economically unviable. This is especially true for light commercial vehicles (LCVs): while BEVs now meet many daily range needs, barriers persist – notably limited access to affordable home charging, increasing reliance on costly fast-charging. [...] A more flexible, incentive-based approach would better support tailored decarbonisation strategies while preserving operational efficiency and competitiveness across the EU. In several member states, there is a notable higher uptake of ZEV in corporate fleets, such as in Belgium. They didn’t use national/EU mandates but focussed on improving the TCO of ZEV in corporate fleets by: • Long-term fiscal frameworks for fleet managers and employees • Tax deductibility for BEVs (with a role for PHEVs) and charging infrastructure • Government co-investment in grid and charging upgrades The European Commission also identifies fiscal measures as one of the more impactful actions to boost demand of zero emission vehicles in its Communication on Decarbonising Corporate Fleets. At the same time, the lack of incentives or its withdrawal immediately leads to less sales as was the case in Germany or France for 2024. A ZEV mandate for Corporate Fleets would be counter productive Introducing binding EU targets for corporate fleet electrification, directly on Corporate fleets or indirectly via targets on Member States, without enabling conditions or pan-EU purchase incentive scheme will not achieve the policy objective as the share of new electrified vehicles (BEVs and PHEVs) is still critically dependent on fiscal incentives provided by national governments. Risks include: Residual Value Collapse [...] “Havana Effect": as a consequence of the above, consumers and companies will delay purchases to avoid costly BEVs, slowing fleet renewal. [...] This would also have an immediate effect on the demand for new vehicles which negatively impacts the entire automotive value chain [...] Companies could simply drop the benefit of company cars and switch to other benefits [...] Lower demand would also make it for OEMs more challenging to comply with the EU fleet CO2 emission reduction targets. A ZEV mandate would also go against the technological neutrality principle the European Commission committed to as part of the Automotive Action Plan presented in March 2025. To conclude, forcing electrification without support creates artificial pressure on vehicle makers while offering no tangible incentive to consumer. This leads to lower registrations, aging fleets, higher costs, value chain impact and rising emissions.

evidence.source_extract: Toyota Motor Corporation Australia (Toyota) welcomes the increased uptake of electric vehicles in Australia and recognises the important role EVs have to play in the motoring needs of Australians, while providing customer choice. Toyota appreciates that the Terms of Reference acknowledge the significant challenges facing EVs to be able to achieve mass market and cross-model adoption, including battery-material shortages, less-than adequate charging infrastructure and the ability to meet diverse customer needs such as towing and a longer driving range [...] Toyota recommends the Government take a broad-based approach that recognises that the Australian market and context requires a range of technologies to reduce vehicle tailpipe emissions. [...] Toyota’s position is that government policies should recognise the benefits of the many electrified powertrains available to reduce tailpipe emissions, including PHEVs, BEVs and FCEVs. In addition, HEVs and emerging technologies such as e-fuels and biofuels will also have an important role to play. In summary: 1. A holistic approach should be taken with regards to the establishment of the resources, systems and infrastructure required to support an increased transition to EVs, that addresses both supply and demand considerations. 2. Government should introduce measures to increase consumer acceptance, that bridge the gap to the price premiums applicable to new technology. Other considerations that government should take into account include: a. The importance (and current inability in a practical manner) of EVs being able to meet diverse customer needs such as towing heavy loads; and b. Whole of vehicle life costs. 3. Given Australia’s vast landscape, infrastructure is critical to EV adoption. While EVs are often a practical solution in cities, significant investment is particularly required in regional Australia to make EVs both a practical and safe motoring option. [...] In addition, the Government should also consider demand-side measures such as provision for: - Demand side incentives that have been successfully implemented to support the transition to BEV and other ZLEVs in countries such as the USA and Europe (Consumer-support mechanisms such as grants, tax credits and other incentives). We expect ZLEV technology to continue to grow in popularity and demand, however our previous experience from the introduction of hybrid shows the transition will take considerable time in the mass market and can only occur with the right focus on education, affordability and infrastructure. [...] Hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) and plug-in hybrid vehicle (PHEV) technology combines an electric motor and battery (also found in BEVs) with an internal combustion engine (ICE) to offer significant fuel savings compared to traditional ICE-only vehicles, at a minimal upfront cost increase. HEVs and PHEVs may be a preferable option for consumers in outer suburban and regional areas where EV charging infrastructure is limite [...] It is also widely reported that there has been slowing consumer take-up of BEVs in the USA and Europe, in part due to the infrastructure not matching market needs. Toyota reiterates again the importance of infrastructure development to support consumer confidence in the transition to BEVs and ZLEVs. [...] There is significant research, development and evaluation underway across industry to develop suitable ZLEVs in the larger SUV and LCV segments; however, it remains challenging and requires significant time and investment. Key customer requirements for larger SUVs and LCVs in Australia include: • Range • Payload • Towing • Off-road capabilities [...] Particular consideration needs to be given to this segment and in particular to the policy levers and/or support the government introduces, and how Australians rely on these vehicles in Australia for their work and livelihoods to support an orderly transition. Without these considerations, there is potential for unintended consequences which could ultimately be to the detriment of consumers and the government’s policy objectives, such as: 1. Vehicle price rises, 2. Companies rationalising their product offerings, or exiting the Australian market resulting in reduced competition and consumer choice, 3. Increased aging of the Australian fleet

evidence.source_extract: The policy and initiatives on synthetic fuels explained by Director Nagai of the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy are truly important. While we have been working toward CO2 reduction and carbon neutrality, we must not forget that the prosperity of humanity worldwide has been built on the accessible and affordable supply of petroleum and energy. Building on this understanding, particularly in the automotive sector, there has been an overemphasis on the "Tank-to-Wheel" perspective. However, achieving true CO2 reduction requires a "Well-to-Wheel" approach. Considering the effective use of battery resources, it is crucial to continue leveraging liquid fuels, which are highly effective for "storing and transporting" energy, to achieve genuine carbon neutrality. Additionally, the concept of "multi-pathway," advocated by the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA), is essential. This approach involves appropriately balancing the use of electricity and fuel according to regions and users, thereby accelerating the realization of carbon neutrality and contributing to greater societal well-being. We support the proposed policy for expanding the adoption of bioethanol. In pursuit of carbon neutrality, JAMA is committed to reducing CO2 swiftly using existing technologies. One such measure is the prompt utilization of biofuels, which, if proven affordable, should include considerations for direct blending, as is already practiced internationally. To this end, as previously mentioned, it is vital for the automotive sector to implement measures such as enabling new vehicles to support E20 fuel blends as early as possible in the 2030s. Biofuels and carbon-neutral fuels are also critical from the perspectives of energy security and resilience. Their adoption will showcase future potential both globally and domestically. Without this, there is a risk of stagnation in areas such as fuel suppliers, service stations, and internal combustion engine development. Therefore, JAMA is committed to working toward the goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 through a strategic combination of biofuels and e-fuels, ensuring the most effective and swift CO2 reductions. To achieve this, we will promptly collaborate with the government and relevant stakeholders to assess whether a phased approach, such as E3, E10, and E20, is necessary and act accordingly.

evidence.im_comment: Supporting specific measures toward clean hydrogen production with major exceptions: directly advocating for weaker implementation guidelines around the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean hydrogen tax credit. Advocating against additionality criteria, a mechanism that ensures hydrogen project consume energy derived from new projects only and do not consume significant current renewable energy capacity. Arguing that additionality is overly restrictive and risks slowing development of clean hydrogen production (Industry Letter on Section 45V Clean Hydrogen Production Tax Credit Implementation, May 2023)
evidence.source_extract: It is the view of the undersigned companies and organizations that the lifecycle analysis calculation must include the use of market-based mechanisms such as renewable energy credits (REC), power purchase agreements (PPAs), or energy attribute certificates (EACs) without any additionality restrictions. The concept of additionality suggests that hydrogen producers can recognize clean electricity and feedstocks used in their processes only if it is derived from new projects. To do so would significantly stifle the clean hydrogen market by adding unreasonable costs and delays for clean hydrogen producers, running counter to the IRA and undermining its economic, jobs, and environmental benefits. In principle, the clean hydrogen industry has the same end goal as additionality proponents: increasing deployment of clean energy. The issue is the proposed mechanism. The timelines for clean hydrogen scale up and siting are not the same as the timelines for new solar, wind or biogas installations, let alone nuclear and hydropower facilities, and to link their implementation negates the independent path clean hydrogen needs to complement these other resources in the drive to decarbonize. This approach defeats the goal of additionality by delaying the clean hydrogen roll out, which is much farther behind than deployment of renewables. It is better to incentivize both clean hydrogen and renewables separately, and let the increased capacity of both technologies work to drive decarbonization faster. The intent of the IRA to grow the hydrogen industry and its potential for large-scale decarbonization will be unfulfilled should additionality requirements be implemented. [...] Any requirements that diminish the value of the credit for electrolyzers would slow development of clean hydrogen production. Potential Economic and Job Loss The United States has seen a massive interest and proposed investment in clean hydrogen manufacturing and production since the enactment of this credit. Unlike other interventions in the rest of the world, these investments are predicated on the premise that this credit would be simple to implement. Should the credit be implemented in a way that provides unnecessary restrictions, such as additionality, there could be potential to reverse some of these manufacturing initiatives, resulting in a significant loss of economic growth, clean manufacturing, and good-paying jobs, diminishing the impact of the IRA as intended.

evidence.im_comment: Opposing the introduction of a zero-emissions vehicle mandate in Canada, advocating for the introduction of flexibilities such as compliance credits to meet ZEV mandates that weaken the stringency of the proposal and reducing the PHEV electric-only requirement to 50km (Response to Canadian consultation on Amending the Passenger Automobile and Light Truck Greenhouse Gas Emission Regulations, March 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Toyota does not support a ZEV mandate because we are concerned that it will not meet its policy objective: meeting carbon emissions reduction targets. The proposed federal ZEV mandate will also lead to unintended bad outcomes for Canadians by making emissions-reducing vehicles more expensive and less accessible. The mandate, as currently designed, could also stifle emissions-reducing innovations and incentivize companies to build plants outside of Canada. Sales mandates by themselves are only forced sales ratios. They do not, on their own, create the necessary conditions that increase supply of electrified products on a faster timeline, that enable ZEV transaction prices offering a strong value proposition for a wide consumer base, or that spur ZEV customer demand. They also do not overcome the current supply chain constrained environment. Alongside this, charging infrastructure and corresponding clean energy availability needs to advance. These issues are not insurmountable, but they will take time and the right conditions to overcome. [...] We also note that one important item missing in this draft mandate, but which is included in the mandates of other jurisdictions, is the ability for OEMs to purchase compliance credits from the government. We offer two proposed solutions: (1) the Federal government should sell compliance credits to companies in need at a fixed, established rate; or (2) the Federal government should be the only source of compliance credits. It could be argued that the companies likely to be in surplus of credits, especially in the early stages of the mandate, will be carmakers who have largely benefited from taxpayer-funded consumer incentives extracted from the Canadian economy without substantially having contributed to it, and will be further monetizing $20,000 or more of economic rent that has been granted to them for each credit, allowing them to extract even more money from the Canadian economy. [...] Proposed Solution #1 – offer early action credits for ZEV sales from the start of the mandate but limit them to incremental increases over the previous model year. Proposed Solution #2 – offer early action credits for ZEV infrastructure investmentsas soon as possible. [...] -Proposed Solution #1 – drop the requirement to 50 kilometers of all-electric range for all PHEVs. This will meet the daily needs of most Canadians and will offer an affordable electrified option for lower-income Canadians and for those that live in rural and remote communities. Proposed Solution #2 – this is more complicated, but create different all-electric range requirements for different vehicle types, with 50 kilometers as the standard for compact and below. [...] Toyota does not support the notion of ZEV mandates because we do not believe they work as intended and can result in unintended consequences. It is a fallacy to believe ZEV Mandates guarantee supply: they prioritize allocation on behalf of some markets at the expense of other markets.

evidence.source_extract: However, the Proposed Rule would force about 60% BEVs alone by 2030, and 67% by 2032. Recent legislation and incentives are directionally supportive but appear far short of what is needed. EPA should adjust the standards in the proposed rule to account for these major uncertainties over which automakers have little control, but for which we face significant compliance and brand/reputation ramifications should they not come to bear. evidence.im_comment: Advocating for 2024 to be a monitoring year only for the UK zero-emission vehicle mandate, advocating to weaken the proposed trajectory for cars, while emphasizing concerns around the proposed trajectory for vans and advocating for numerous flexibilities that may weaken the stringency of the proposal (Toyota response to UK government consultation on ZEV mandate and CO2 emissions regulation for new cars and vans, found via FOI request, May 2023)
evidence.source_extract: Toyota is not against the introduction of the ZEV mandate. However, the proposals put forward present the company with challenges, for which it seeks flexibility or accommodation, particularly in the initial three years, 2024 to 2026. Following this final consultation, there will be only a few weeks or months before mandate comes into force in 2024. For businesses to plan and make the changes necessary to meet the mandate’s requirements, a period of at least 12 months should be allowed. The proposed speed of introduction is potentially too fast for local manufacturing to support, risking an increase in vehicle imports from countries which use carbon-intensive production methods. Toyota is also concerned that despite having established leadership in reducing CO2 emissions using a range of technologies, it will be more exposed to penalties. The level of proposed penalties would have a seriously negative impact on a leading manufacturer during a critical transition period for the UK automotive industry – a time when enhancing business competitiveness will be essential. [...] Toyota cannot meet the requirements of the mandate in the period 2024 to 2026 because of its successful multi-path technology strategy, so seeks flexibility beyond that currently being proposed. It welcomes the arrangements for banking and borrowing and the mechanism for transferring non-ZEV to ZEV performance, but these provisions are inadequate during the initial phase for all manufacturers. [...] Toyota will be ready to meet the target of 80% ZEV new vehicle sales in the UK in 2030. By making additional efforts, it also expects to be fully compliant with the ZEV mandate targets and trajectory by 2027 and it will deliver on the goal of all its new UK vehicle sales being ZEVs in 2035. However, the trajectory proposed for the early years, 2024 to 2026, is not possible for Toyota to meet in full and will be unfairly punitive to a manufacturer that is a long-established industry leader in reducing CO2 emissions. Toyota proposes 2024 should be a monitoring-only year, with no imposition of penalties. This will give manufacturers the opportunity to gauge the impact of the mandate on their business and commence the process of adapting accordingly. [...] Under the current proposals, the company thus faces the prospect of having to pay severe trading penalties running into hundreds of millions of pounds during this period, harming its hard-earned competitiveness and impacting its well-founded and long-standing global environmental reputation. [...] Toyota seeks additional flexibility in the transfer of non-ZEV to ZEV sales in the early years of the mandate, 2024 to 2026. It considers the initial cap of 25% non-ZEV sales is too restrictive and proposes starting at higher rate, 65%, declining progressively to 45% then 25% in year three. [...] Toyota supports the SMMT’s call for the Government to take a “monitoring only” approach during the first year of the ZEV mandate in 2024. [...] While Toyota considers the trajectory proposed for zero emission vans to be more manageable than that for cars, it presents the same fundamental issues, in particular the impact during the initial years, 2024 to 2026. As with passenger vehicles, the product cycles for vans are between five and seven years; at such short notice, these cycles cannot be changed. We therefore propose that 2024 should be a monitoring year.

evidence.im_comment: Opposing California's proposed Advanced Clean Cars II regulation, which would require an increasing percentage of new light-duty EV sales each year until a 100% ZEV mandate in 2035; advocating for numerous flexibilities, a biannual review of the program (Toyota comments on California's proposed Advanced Clean Cars II Regulation, May 2022)
evidence.source_extract: The ACC2 regulation is aligned with Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-79-20, which set the ambitious goal of 100% ZEV sales by 2035. And while consumer interest in ZEV technologies is growing, we are concerned about the 2026MY starting requirement of 35% and the pace of increase year-over-year thereafter. […] The ACC2 requirement would force the ZEV market to move to the mainstream quickly. This means we need ZEV product in the Camry/RAV4 price range, around low to mid $30,000. Other challenges include procurement and cost of raw materials for electrical components, the ability to ramp up battery production, and the development of an ecosystem to manage end-of-life batteries from all these ZEVs. Lastly, electric charging and hydrogen refueling infrastructure needs to advance to support these ambitious goals. In conclusion, while purchase cost is an important factor for mainstream customers there are multiple, complex factors at play that are outside Toyota’s or California’s ability to control that make ACC2 an extraordinary challenge to meet. As difficult a challenge it is to comply with this proposed regulation in California, it is more difficult in S177 states. […] we urge CARB to maintain the travel provision, but with the following limitations to address S177 state concerns : • Sunset travel after 2030, • Cap travel credit usage to 10% of an OEM requirement in a S177 state, and • Phase-out travel as infrastructure in S177 states catches up to the California baseline of hydrogen readiness. […] Toyota supports the goals of electrification and the transformation of the light duty vehicle fleet, but we have significant concerns with the pace and volume requirements of the staff’s proposal. The ZEV and PHEV markets have been moving quickly and continue to evolve. Despite cost and market breakthroughs, industry sales in 2021 were only 13% (albeit increasing to 16% in Q1 2022) and about 5% in S177 states. We have a long way to go to reach the ambitious targets CARB expects in ACC2, and the fundamental question remains how quickly the vast majority of California and S177 state drivers will embrace these technologies and products. For these reasons, we urge the Board to consider a formal and periodic review of the ZEV program, including both technology and market considerations. This will allow CARB to continue to adjust and allow for new considerations as the market, consumer demand, and innovation evolves. We believe this review should occur biannually, and that CARB should engage both market and technology experts to provide independent analysis.

evidence.im_comment: Opposing federal US heavy-duty zero-emision vehicle mandates (Toyota comments on US Control of Air Pollution from New Motor Vehicles: Heavy Duty Engine and Vehicle Standards, May 2022)
evidence.source_extract: HD Zero Emission Vehicles (ZEV) Mandate not Feasible without Additional Investments. EPA has indicated that it is not considering a HD ZEV mandate at this time. Toyota supports this approach. A ZEV mandate for light-duty vehicles exists in California and other states that have adopted California’s regulations. In addition, other federal regulations such as EPA’s light-duty greenhouse gas (GHG) regulations and NHTSA’s related Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) regulations are compelling a greater need for light-duty zero-emission technologies. Achieving these existing regulations requires complementary market-development and sustainment measures, including infrastructure investments for electric vehicle charging and hydrogen refueling, critical mineral supply chain development, and a robust system to recycle end-of-life vehicle batteries. Adding a Federal HD vehicle mandate on top of existing light-duty mandates will exacerbate each of these challenges and could put successful compliance with ZEV mandates in both sectors in jeopardy.

evidence.im_comment: Evidence suggests not supporting California's Advanced Clean Fleets regulation that includes a 100% ZEV sales mandate for medium and heavy-duty vehicles in 2040; emphasizing concerns and potential negative impacts on company's operations (Toyota Comments on proposed Advanced Clean Fleets Regulation, October 2022)
evidence.source_extract: Toyota believes the ACF regulation will have an enormous impact on both the environment and the economy. There will be environmental benefit with ZE trucks on the road, but also operational trade-offs. As an example, Toyota and its logistic partners, operate auto carriers to deliver vehicles to dealerships. The current diesel-powered auto carriers can carry - on average - eight vehicles per truck. The transition to ZE auto carriers would decrease the load allowance to six vehicles due to physical limitations (e.g., no vehicle placement over truck cab and/or weight restrictions). Toyota estimates that for every diesel auto carrier replaced, 1.2 ZE (Battery or FC) auto carriers is needed. In other words, Toyota would need to make approximately 20% more truck trips to carry the same number of vehicles. With the sale of 300,000 Toyota vehicles/year in California, the seemingly small difference in vehicles per truckload can amount to significant costs and disruptions to our business operations. It would also increase the number of heavy-duty trucks on California roadways by 20% and contribute to additional traffic congestion. Toyota requests CARB take a “balanced” approach that drives emissions improvements, while doing so as economically as possible. Toyota agrees with the State that technology will ultimately drive the transition to carbon neutrality. However, this transition requires careful consideration around the time needed to develop new infrastructure, implement new driver/workforce training, and adjust business models.

All these alternatives will help in the pursuit of lower carbon. The narrow focus on BEVs as the only solution stems from the view that they must be the most carbon friendly since they burn no gasoline. It’s true that if you compare an average hybrid, plug-in hybrid, BEV and fuel cell electric, you’ll generally find that BEVs and fuel cells are the lowest emitting, followed by plug-in hybrids and hybrids. While true in many cases, it’s not true across the board...last year, less than 2% of the vehicles sold in America were battery electric. If we are to make dramatic progress in electrification, it will require overcoming tremendous challenges, including refuelling infrastructure, battery availability, consumer acceptance and affordability, and the reliability of the electric grid...Without doubt, technology-inclusive policies will provide more Americans with more electrified options and will likely achieve greater GHG benefits as a result. [...] Without doubt, technology-inclusive policies will provide more Americans with more electrified options and will likely achieve greater GHG benefits as a result.The policy with the greatest immediate impact on sales is consumer purchase incentives. These incentives should be structured to promote all electrified vehicles, allow consumer choice, and provide greater opportunity for GHG reductions than a single pathway can provide. And these incentives can’t sunset too quickly or they won’t provide investment certainty manufactures need.

evidence.im_comment: Directly advocating to policymakers to oppose an ICE ban in New Zealand and a 40% EV fleet target for 2035 (Response to consultation to New Zealand's Climate Change Commission, March 2021)
evidence.source_extract: Toyota recommends that the Commission re-think its path for transport because the target for the uptake of Electric Vehicles (EVs) is not achievable. [...] Provide for the progressive transition to low-emissions vehicles, including but not limited to increased use of EVs. Adopt a threshold and criteria for when the Government would set a target to ban further importation of ICEs. [...] The path proposed by the Commission for transport is flawed and will not deliver the expected results. There is a better way. A more comprehensive, system-focused and progressive plan is needed for the transport system to achieve the intended reduction in emissions. The target for the light vehicle fleet is not achievable under the proposed time frame and will have unintended effects.Our primary concern with the Commission’s path for transport is that the target for the light vehicle fleet is not achievable. It will not be possible to achieve the target of 40 percent of the fleet being EVs by 2035. Toyota cannot achieve this target without there being serious and perverse outcomes for kiwis over the short term. Given Toyota’s global leadership in hybrid electric technology, if we can’t achieve the target, then it is likely that other vehicle suppliers will also be unable to do so. [...] If the proposed path is not changed, it will lead to perverse outcomes. This could include: • The importation of second hand EVs from markets that permit lower safety standards. • Kiwi families and businesses will be forced to keep their older, high emissions and less safe vehicles for longer. • Suppliers will be forced to discontinue non-EV models that are essential for certain segments of our community. [...] Toyota New Zealand therefore believes that the path for reducing emissions from the light vehicle will be far more effective if it is technology agnostic. It should be designed to incentivise continual reductions in emissions from the fleet without dictating which technologies should be adopted to achieve this outcome. Instead, it should support new, cleaner, and safer vehicles progressively coming into the market at a competitive price that is affordable for kiwis. While the EV tax proposal before you makes strides toward that goal, it includes provisions that will discriminate against nearly half the autoworkers in the country and puts the environment second to unrelated agendas. First, the proposal to provide a $4,500 additional incentive exclusively for union-built EVs runs counter to the goal of carbon reduction. To state the obvious, an EV made by autoworkers who choose to unionize does not make that vehicle any better for the environment. [...] Second, we urge you to reject using the country’s limited resources to give exorbitant tax breaks to those wealthy enough to buy high-priced cars and trucks. Today, electric vehicles (EVs) cost more to make than conventional automobiles. The resulting price premium puts EVs out of reach for many Americans. But electric cars shouldn’t just be for rich people. The proposed $7,500 tax credit for EVs makes these vehicles more accessible to Americans of modest means, and we support it. However, we question the proposal to offer tax incentives of up to $12,500 for the purchase of vehicles that are priced as high as $70,000. Given the competing social priorities the “Build Back Better” plan is intended to address, does it make sense to give a tax break of $12,500 to people who can afford to spend as much on a vehicle as some Americans spend on a home? Toyota believes that the emphasis should be on making all EVs, including the newest models with superior safety and emission reductions, affordable to all Americans, not just the wealthy.

[...] While Toyota believes the problem we’re trying to address is the cumulative emissions of the Canadian on-road fleet, the activity should be focused on reducing “Carbon Kilometers Travelled”. Simply, this is the rate of emissions of a vehicle x the distanced travelled. There are two factors that need to be addressed – reducing the rate of emissions, which could be addressed by migrating to more fuel-efficient vehicles (particularly in commercial, taxi or ride hailing fleets) - or by reducing the number of kilometers travelled, which could be addressed through a variety of means including such things as energy pricing, tiered licensing or insurance, or increasing the availability of mass transit. The two factors can be addressed individually or together. A ZEV mandate does not adequately address either of those problems for the reasons explained below. [...] Consideration 2: ZEV programs, on their own, do not work There are many global jurisdictions, ranging from national to sub-national (and even local) – where effective policy has seen an increase in ZEV uptake and a decrease in overall emissions. While some of these jurisdictions have set a goal for an ICE ban ranging from 2035 to 2040, they are not focusing only on one potential technological solution. [...] With respect to Quebec, the province brought into force its provincial ZEV mandate in 2019. Over that time, consumer trends have continued to veer towards large (and greater emitting vehicles) such as pick-ups and SUVs - vehicle segments that currently do not have an adequate ZEV solution. [...] One of the more frustrating aspects of a ZEV mandate – from the point of view of an OEM – is the focus on the act of selling a specific vehicle technology. [...] While Canada’s high-level priorities are aligned with Toyota’s– a mutual goal to increase electrification and decrease GHG emissions from our automobiles – we recommend a more wideranging and balanced set of policy objectives rather than a singular focus on ZEV adoption. Remain technology-neutral and focus on overall emissions reduction strategies. All emissions reduction strategies should be considered. So should mass transit. 3. Recognize that Canadian trade policy and a desire to manufacture (more) electrified vehicles in Canada are currently in direct conflict. 4. Listen to the experts in industry, not only special interest groups.

Such an approach will also enable the EU to unlock the wall of private capital needed to meet its investment needs. At the same time, policies should support an increased supply and demand for low carbon materials. Enhancing Energy Security with the Clean Energy Transition The target will support the EU’s overall strategy to deeply enhance energy security for citizens and businesses by accelerating the clean energy transition and energy efficiency. [...] We call for the EU to set a policy environment that will phase out fossil fuels, accelerate electrification and the decarbonisation of the power sector with renewables and low-carbon electricity, ensure access to flexible energy infrastructure, and large scale roll out of energy efficiency measures in industry and buildings. In this context, robust carbon pricing should continue to incentivise investments in decarbonised energy and solutions. Fossil fuels subsidies should be eliminated, freeing up finance to be reallocated for the development of clean technologies. Stepping up Implementation As we enter two decisive decades to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, the EU needs to build on the legacy of the Green Deal and an effective implementation of the Fit for 55 Package. Businesses are ready to play a key role in translating climate targets into concrete action with the support of enabling measures and policies. They are taking action to decarbonise their operations and value chains by increasing efficient use of energy, switching to low-carbon energy, transitioning to electric vehicles and developing low-carbon materials. Meanwhile, many investors are setting net zero strategies and working to integrate climate risks and opportunities into their individual investment decisions and processes.

evidence.source_extract: We urge: Financial institutions to work collaboratively with us, and with policymakers, to ensure that capital is being allocated to accelerate the clean energy transition — creating a financial system that safeguards future growth and returns for people and planet. evidence.query: Climate Science Stance: Does the organization support a science-based response to the climate crisis?
evidence.im_comment: Supporting action to achieve zero carbon economies by 2050 (The Investor Agenda, 2024 Global Investor Statement to Governments on the Climate Crisis, September 2024).
evidence.source_extract: The 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28) reaffirmed the need for urgent action to achieve the ambition of the Paris Agreement and limit global temperature rise to 1.5ºC above pre-industrial levels. In a landmark decision, the First Global Stocktake was concluded at COP28, with nearly 200 countries unanimously agreeing to support a just and equitable transition away from fossil fuels, and to accelerate the shift towards net zero emission energy systems by 2050. The consensus decision also called for an interim goal of tripling renewable energy and doubling energy efficiency globally by 2030, as well as conserving, protecting, and restoring nature and ecosystems to meet international climate goals [...] Effective policies are essential at all levels of government to accelerate the private capital flows needed for a climate-resilient, nature-positive, just net zero transition. Therefore, we encourage a whole-of-government approach to implement policies in line with countries’ nationally-determined contributions (NDCs) and a 1.5°C scenario, recognizing common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities between emerging and developed economies, that will accelerate private sector action and large-scale investment.
